name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 1: Review of Lesson 3

questiontext.text:
Section 1: Review of Lesson 3

Quick Summary

In Lesson 3, we examined the Peal Perfect tense (the suffix conjugation), learning how Syriac describes completed, past actions. The sentence structure shifted from fluidly subject-led (in the present participle) to stringently Verb-Subject-Object (VSO) led narrative chains using the conjunction w- (and).

5-Question Warm-Up Drill

(Answers in Section 9)

  1. What does the final Waw of ܟܬܒܘ (ktab(w)) indicate, and how is it pronounced?
  2. Translate the basic VSO sentence: Šbaq malkā l-ʾarʿā.
  3. What happens to the pronunciation of k-t-b (ka-tab) in the Syriac 3rd m.sg Perfect?
  4. How do you distinguish between “I wrote” and “You (m) wrote” if both are written ܟܬܒܬ (ktabt/ketbet) without vowels?
  5. Translate: w-qreb Yūḥannan.
Warm-up 1. What does the final Waw of ܟܬܒܘ (ktab(w)) indicate?

generalfeedback.text: The Perfect is the suffix conjugation: person is marked at the end of the verb, and the silent Waw marks 3 m.pl.

feedback.text: Right: ktab(w) = “they wrote.” The Waw is written but silent.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 2. Translate: Šbaq malkā l-ʾarʿā.

feedback.text: In VSO order the noun right after the verb is the subject; l- marks the object.
Šbaq is Perfect (completed action), so English needs a past tense.

answer.text: The king will leave the earth.

feedback.text: The future/Imperfect is not introduced until Lesson 8; šbaq is Perfect.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 3. What happens to the vowels of k-t-b in the 3rd m.sg. Perfect?

generalfeedback.text: Vowel reduction is a hallmark of Syriac compared with Hebrew and Arabic.

answer.text: The vowel after the first radical drops (vowel reduction), giving ktab.

feedback.text: Right: Syriac reduces the short vowel in the open first syllable, so not *katab but ktab.
Katab is the Hebrew/Arabic shape; Syriac reduces the first vowel.
Prefixes belong to the Imperfect, not the Perfect.

answer.text: The middle radical is doubled, giving kattab.

feedback.text: Doubling marks the Pael stem (Lesson 6), not the Peal Perfect.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 4. Unvocalized ܟܬܒܬ can mean “I wrote” or “you (m) wrote.” How do you tell them apart?

generalfeedback.text: Ambiguous consonantal forms are resolved by context or by vowel points.

answer.text: Only by context or vowel pointing.

feedback.text: Right: the consonants are identical (ketbet vs ktabt).
No extra letter is written; the spelling is the same.
w- means “and” and has nothing to do with person.

answer.text: They cannot be told apart at all.

feedback.text: Readers rely on context, and vocalized texts mark the difference with points.

questiontext.text: Warm-up 5. Translate: w-qreb Yūḥannan.

feedback.text: Qreb is a Perfect verb, not an adjective.

answer.text: And they drew near to Yukhannan.

feedback.text: “They” would require the plural (qreb(w), written with a final Waw).

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 2: Possession and Pronominal Suffixes — Overview

questiontext.text:
Section 2: Possession and Pronominal Suffixes — Overview

In English, we indicate possession using separate pronouns placed before a noun: “my house”, “your king”. In Greek, it’s often an independent genitive pronoun: ὁ οἶκός μου (ho oikos mou).

However, in Semitic languages, possession is expressed by attaching a pronominal suffix directly to the end of the noun.

Cross-Linguistic Comparison: The Possessive Suffix

  • Hebrew: סוּס (sūs, horse) → סוּסִי (sūsī, my horse). אָב (ʾāb, father) → אָבִינוּ (ʾābīnū, our father).
  • Arabic: كتاب (kitāb, book) → كتابي (kitābī, my book).
  • Syriac: ܟܬܒ (ktāb, book) → ܟܬܒܝ (ktāb(y), my book). ܐܒ (ʾab, father) → ܐܒܘܢ (ʾabūn, our father).

These suffixes are derived from the same ancient roots as the independent pronouns (ʾenā, ʾant, hū) but are highly compressed.

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 3: Pronominal Suffixes on Nouns & Prepositions

questiontext.text:
Section 3: Pronominal Suffixes on Nouns & Prepositions

1. Suffixes on Singular Nouns

To add a suffix, Syriac drops the Emphatic state ending (-ā) and attaches the suffix to the bound/construct stem of the noun. (You don’t say “the my-king” *malkā-y; you say “king-my”, malk(y)).

  • Malk- (king) + -eh (his) = malkeh (his king).
  • ʾAb- (father) + -y (my) = ʾab(y) (my father).

The 1 c.sg. suffix on a singular noun is a Yodh that is written but silent: ܡܠܟܝ “my king” is pronounced malk, and ܐܒܝ “my father” ʾāb. The transliteration shows it in parentheses: malk(y).

2. Suffixes on Prepositions

The exact same suffixes attach to the inseparable prepositions b- (in) and l- (to/for).

  • b- + -eh = beh (in him / in it).
  • l- + -k = lāk (to you, m.sg).

3. The Idiom for “To Have”

Syriac (like Hebrew and Arabic) lacks a dedicated verb meaning “to possess” (like English “to have” or Latin “habere”). Instead, Semitic languages use a prepositional phrase: “there is to me” or just “to me”.

  • ʾīt lī (there-is to-me) → ʾīt lī = I have.
  • layt leh (there-is-not to-him) = He does not have.
  • ʾīt lī šrārā = I have truth. (Lit: There is to me truth).

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 4: The Suffix Paradigm for Singular Nouns

questiontext.text:
Section 4: The Suffix Paradigm for Singular Nouns

This paradigm uses the masculine noun malk- (king, root m-l-k) and the feminine noun malkūt- (kingdom). Notice the suffix column; you must memorize these endings.

Person Suffix Masculine Noun (malk-) Translit Fem Noun (malkūt-) Translit
1 c.sg. (my) ـܝ (silent -y) ܡܠܟܝ malk(y) ܡܠܟܘܬܝ malkūt(y)
2 m.sg. (your) ـܟ (-k) ܡܠܟܟ malk-āk ܡܠܟܘܬܟ malkūt-āk
2 f.sg. (your) ـܟܝ (-ky) ܡܠܟܟܝ malk-ēk(y) ܡܠܟܘܬܟܝ malkūt-ēk(y)
3 m.sg. (his) ـܗ (-eh) ܡܠܟܗ malk-eh ܡܠܟܘܬܗ malkūt-eh
3 f.sg. (her) ـܗ (-āh) ܡܠܟܗ malk-āh ܡܠܟܘܬܗ malkūt-āh
1 c.pl. (our) ـܢ (-n) ܡܠܟܢ malk-an ܡܠܟܘܬܢ malkūt-an
2 m.pl. (your) ـܟܘܢ (-kūn) ܡܠܟܟܘܢ malk-kūn ܡܠܟܘܬܟܘܢ malkūt-kūn
2 f.pl. (your) ـܟܝܢ (-kēn) ܡܠܟܟܝܢ malk-kēn ܡܠܟܘܬܟܝܢ malkūt-kēn
3 m.pl. (their) ـܗܘܢ (-hūn) ܡܠܟܗܘܢ malk-hūn ܡܠܟܘܬܗܘܢ malkūt-hūn
3 f.pl. (their) ـܗܝܢ (-hēn) ܡܠܟܗܝܢ malk-hēn ܡܠܟܘܬܗܝܢ malkūt-hēn

Orthography Note: The 3rd masculine singular (-eh) and 3rd feminine singular (-āh) are both spelled with a final He (ܗ). Only vowel pointing or context distinguishes “his” from “her”.

Suffixes on Plural Nouns

A plural noun takes a slightly different set of suffixes, with a linking -ay-. You have already met talmīdaw(hy) “his disciples”. The forms, on ܡ̈ܠܟܐ malkē “kings”:

Person Estrangela Transliteration Meaning
1 c.sg. ܡ̈ܠܟܝ malkay my kings
2 m.sg. ܡ̈ܠܟܝܟ malkayk your (m.sg.) kings
2 f.sg. ܡ̈ܠܟܝܟܝ malkayk(y) your (f.sg.) kings
3 m.sg. ܡ̈ܠܟܘܗܝ malkaw(hy) his kings
3 f.sg. ܡ̈ܠܟܝܗ malkēh her kings
1 c.pl. ܡ̈ܠܟܝܢ malkayn our kings
2 m.pl. ܡ̈ܠܟܝܟܘܢ malkaykūn your (m.pl.) kings
3 m.pl. ܡ̈ܠܟܝܗܘܢ malkayhūn their (m.) kings

Several prepositions take this plural set even though they are not plural: ʿal “upon” (ʿlaw(hy) “upon him”), qdām “before” (qdāmaw(hy) “before him”). The particle ʾīt does the same: ʾītaw(hy) “he is, it is”.

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 5: Prepositional "To Have" Paradigm (l- + Suffix)

questiontext.text:
Section 5: Prepositional "To Have" Paradigm (l- + Suffix)

How to say “I have”, “You have”, “He has”, etc., by attaching suffixes to the l- preposition, often preceded by ʾīt (there is).

Person Estrangela (l- + suffix) Transliteration Meaning
1 c.sg. ܠܝ lī to me (I have)
2 m.sg. ܠܟ lāk to you (You [m.sg.] have)
2 f.sg. ܠܟܝ lēk(y) to you (You [f.sg.] have)
3 m.sg. ܠܗ leh to him (He has)
3 f.sg. ܠܗ lāh to her (She has)
1 c.pl. ܠܢ lan to us (We have)
2 m.pl. ܠܟܘܢ lkūn to you (You [m.pl.] have)
2 f.pl. ܠܟܝܢ lkēn to you (You [f.pl.] have)
3 m.pl. ܠܗܘܢ lhūn to them (They [m.pl.] have)
3 f.pl. ܠܗܝܢ lhēn to them (They [f.pl.] have)

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 6: Vocabulary (Family, Body Parts & Belongings)

questiontext.text:
Section 6: Vocabulary (Family, Body Parts & Belongings)

Family and body parts are the most common nouns to receive pronominal suffixes. (Note: ʾabā ‘father’ and ʾaḥā ‘brother’ insert -ū- before suffixes other than 1 c.sg., e.g. ʾabūk ‘your father’, ʾabū(hy) ‘his father’).

Construct / Emphatic Transliteration Meaning Example with Suffix (1 c.sg.)
ܐܒ / ܐܒܐ ʾab / ʾabā Father ʾab(y) (my father)
ܐܡ / ܐܡܐ ʾem / ʾemmā Mother ʾem(y) (my mother)
ܒܪ / ܒܪܐ bar / brā Son ber(y) (my son; note the vowel: breh his son, brāk your son)
ܒܪܬ / ܒܪܬܐ bart / bartā Daughter brat(y) (my daughter)
ܐܚ / ܐܚܐ ʾaḥ / ʾaḥā Brother ʾaḥ(y) (my brother)
ܐܝܕ / ܐܝܕܐ ʾīd / ʾīdā Hand (f) ʾīd(y) (my hand)
ܪܝܫ / ܪܝܫܐ rēš / rēšā Head (m) rēš(y) (my head)
ܩܠ / ܩܠܐ qāl / qālā Voice (m) qāl(y) (my voice)
ܠܒܘܫ / ܠܒܘܫܐ lbūš / lbūšā Garment lbūš(y) (my garment)
ܒܝܬ / ܒܝܬܐ bēt / baytā House bayt(y) (my house)
ܢܛܘܪ / ܢܛܘܪܐ nāṭōr / nāṭōrā Guard, watchman (pl. nāṭōrē) nāṭōr(y) (my guard)
ܡܐ / ܡܢܐ mā / mānā What? (Interrogative pronoun; two forms, not a construct and emphatic)
ܐܝܟܐ ʾaykā Where? (Interrogative adverb; with 3 m.sg. enclitic: ܐܝܟܘ ʾaykaw “where is he?”)

name.text: Module 1 · Lesson 4 · Section 7: The Story — Part 4

questiontext.text:
Section 7: The Story — Part 4

A Dialogue at the Gate

Narrative note: Watch how the guards use suffixes with prepositions (leh, lāk) and nouns (ʾabūk, ʾemmāk) to interrogate Yukhannan about his origins and possessions.

Sentence 1

ܩܡ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܒܬܪܥܐ ܕܡܠܟܘܬܐ qām Yūḥannan b-tarʿā d-malkūtā. qām (stood) Yūḥannan (John) b-tarʿā (in-the-gate) d-malkūtā (of-the-kingdom). → Yukhannan stood at the gate of the kingdom.

Sentence 2

ܘܐܡܪܝܢ ܢܛܘܪ̈ܐ ܕܬܪܥܐ ܠܗ w-ʾāmrīn nāṭōrē d-tarʿā leh: w-ʾāmrīn (and-are-saying) nāṭōrē (the-guards) d-tarʿā (of-the-gate) leh (to-him): → And the guards of the gate say to him:

Sentence 3

ܡܢ ܐܝܢܐ ܐܬܪܐ ܐܢܬ men ʾaynā ʾatrā ʾant? men (from) ʾaynā (what) ʾatrā (country/place) ʾant (you-[are])? → “From what country are you?”

Sentence 4

ܘܐܝܟܐ ܐܒܘܟ ܘܐܡܟ w-ʾaykā ʾab-ūk w-ʾemm-āk? w-ʾaykā (and-where) ʾab-ūk (father-your) w-ʾemm-āk (and-mother-your)? → “And where are your father and your mother?”

Sentence 5

ܘܡܐ ܐܝܬ ܠܟ ܒܐܝܕܟ w-mā ʾīt lāk b-ʾīd-āk? w-mā (and-what) ʾīt (there-is) lāk (to-you) b-ʾīd-āk (in-hand-your)? → “And what do you have in your hand?”

Sentence 6

ܐܡܪ ܠܗܘܢ ܝܘܚܢܢ ʾemar lhūn Yūḥannan: ʾemar (said) lhūn (to-them) Yūḥannan (John): → Yukhannan said to them:

Sentence 7

ܐܠܗܐ ܗܘ ܐܒܝ ܘܐܪܥܐ ܗܝ ܐܡܝ ʾAlāhā hū ʾab(y), w-ʾarʿā hī ʾem(y). ʾAlāhā (God) hū (he-[is]) ʾab(y) (father-my), w-ʾarʿā (and-the-earth) hī (she-[is]) ʾem(y) (mother-my). → “God is my father, and the earth is my mother.”

Sentence 8

ܘܠܝܬ ܠܝ ܒܝܬܐ ܒܐܪܥܐ w-layt lī baytā b-ʾarʿā. w-layt (and-there-is-not) lī (to-me) baytā (a-house) b-ʾarʿā (in-the-land). → “And I have no house in the land.”

Sentence 9

ܢܘܗܪܐ ܕܐܠܗܐ ܐܝܬܘܗܝ ܒܐܝܕܝ nūhrā d-ʾAlāhā ʾītaw(hy) b-ʾīd(y). nūhrā (the-light) d-ʾAlāhā (of-God) ʾītaw(hy) (it-is) b-ʾīd(y) (in-hand-my). → “The light of God is in my hand.”

Sentence 10

ܘܥܠ ܝܘܚܢܢ ܠܡܕܝܢܬܐ w-ʿal Yūḥannan l-mdīttā. w-ʿal (and-entered) Yūḥannan (John) l-mdīttā (into-the-city). → And Yukhannan entered the city.

Story note: ʿal “he entered” behaves like qām in Sentence 1; both are hollow verbs, explained in Lesson 7. In Lesson 5 Yukhannan begins to preach to the crowds inside the city.

Exercise 1. Identify the possessor in ܒܝܬܗ (bayt-eh).

generalfeedback.text: ܗ alone can also be 3 f.sg. -āh “her”; the vocalization -eh makes it “his.”

Exercise 3. Translate: ʾAb(y) ṭāb hū, w-ʾem(y) ṭābā hī.

answer.text: My father is good, and my mother is good.

feedback.text: Right: verbless clauses with hū/hī as copula.

answer.text: His father is good, and his mother is good.
My father is a king, and my mother is a queen.
My father was good, and my mother was good.

feedback.text: The pronoun copula gives a present “is.”

questiontext.text: Exercise 3. Translate: Šbaq(w) talmīdē l-baythūn.
Exercise 3. Translate: ʾĪt lan nūhrā rabbā.

feedback.text: Right: literally “there is to us a great light.”

answer.text: We do not have a great light.

questiontext.text: Exercise 3. Translate: Qālā d-malkā b-ʾarʿan.

answer.text: The voice of the king is in our land.
The voice of the king is in his land.
The king’s word is in our land.
Our king’s voice is in the land.

feedback.text: The suffix is on ʾarʿā, not on malkā.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. Render into Syriac: “My brother is writing a word.”

feedback.text: Ktab is Perfect “wrote”; “is writing” needs the participle.
Kātbā is the feminine participle; “brother” is masculine.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. “The king and his son are going to his kingdom.”

feedback.text: Right: plural participle ʾāzlīn for a compound subject.
ʾEzal is Perfect “went”; “are going” needs the participle.

questiontext.text: Exercise 4. “What is in your (m.sg) hand?”
Exercise 4. “We do not have an evil king.”
Exercise 5 (Section 7). Under what three topics does the guard interrogate Yukhannan?

answer.text: Origin (what country), family (where are his father and mother), and possessions (what is in his hand)
His name, his teacher, and his god

feedback.text: Re-read Section 7: the questions are country, parents and possessions.

answer.text: His language, his books, and his journey
His age, his work, and his house

questiontext.text: Exercise 5. Who does Yukhannan claim as his parents?

feedback.text: Not in this story; re-read Section 7.

questiontext.text: Exercise 5. What does Yukhannan explicitly say he does not have?

answer.text: A house in the land (baytā b-ʾarʿā)

questiontext.text:
Section 10: Grammatical Summary

THE PRONOMINAL SUFFIXES (ATTACH TO NOUNS AND PREPOSITIONS)

Suffix Meaning Example (bayt- house) Example (l- to)
-y my bayt(y) (my house) lī (to me)
-k your (m.sg.) baytāk (your house) lāk (to you)
-ky your (f.sg.) baytēk(y) (your house) lēk(y) (to you)
-eh his bayteh (his house) leh (to him)
-āh her baytāh (her house) lāh (to her)
-an our baytan (our house) lan (to us)
-kūn your (m.pl.) baytkūn (your house) lkūn (to you all)
-kēn your (f.pl.) baytkēn (your house) lkēn (to you all)
-hūn their (m.pl.) baythūn (their house) lhūn (to them)
-hēn their (f.pl.) baythēn (their house) lhēn (to them)

SAYING “TO HAVE” (Possession Formula)

Formula Syriac Meaning
ʾĪT + L- + Suffix ʾīt lī I have (There is to me)
LAYT + L- + Suffix layt leh He does not have
ʾĪT + L- + Suffix ʾīt lhūn malkā They have a king
